strengths: Conceptual novelty: The paper presents an interesting formulation connecting self-supervised pretext pre-training and downstream supervised fine-tuning within a bilevel optimization (BLO) framework.

Mathematical clarity: The derivation of the implicit gradient via the implicit function theorem (following an iMAML-style formulation) is clearly laid out and well-explained in the main text and appendix.

Comprehensive downstream test suite: The evaluation covers 14 downstream image classification datasets with varying characteristics (fine-grained, textures, general objects), reporting both top-1 and top-5 metrics with standard deviations over multiple seeds.
Presentation: The manuscript is clearly structured, with well-documented hyperparameters and reproducible experimental details provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Lack of essential baselines: The paper only compares BiSSL against vanilla fine-tuning ('Only FT'). Crucially, it does not compare against a simple joint/multi-task learning baseline (i.e., simultaneously optimizing the downstream loss and pretext loss $\mathcal{L}^D + \beta \mathcal{L}^P$), leaving it unclear whether bilevel optimization provides tangible advantages over standard multi-task optimization. Furthermore, several existing backbone-priming methods discussed in Section 2 (such as COIN, Noisy-Tune, or RIFLE) are not evaluated.

No runtime or computational complexity analysis: Solving the bilevel problem with implicit differentiation requires iterative Hessian-vector product computations via Conjugate Gradient (CG) for every upper-level update. This introduces substantial computational and memory overhead, yet the paper reports no training runtimes, wall-clock comparisons, or FLOP counts to evaluate the trade-off between computation and performance.

Small-scale experimental setting: Experiments are restricted to a ResNet-18 pre-trained on the small-scale STL-10 dataset (96x96 resolution). In modern self-supervised learning, standard evaluations utilize ImageNet-1k pre-training on standard architectures (e.g., ResNet-50, ViT) and evaluate on standard transfer benchmarks. It remains unproven whether BiSSL is practical or beneficial at standard scales.

Flawed premise in qualitative feature inspection: In Section 4.4 and Figures 3–11, the authors argue that BiSSL better aligns downstream features prior to fine-tuning compared to standard pretext features. However, BiSSL's upper-level objective explicitly optimizes the downstream supervised classification loss using downstream labels. Showing that BiSSL representations cluster better by class than an unsupervised backbone that has never observed downstream labels is expected and does not convincingly isolate the specific benefit of the bilevel mechanism over direct supervision.

Pipeline complexity for modest gains: The overall workflow requires four distinct stages (pretext warm-up, downstream head warm-up, BiSSL alternating optimization with ad-hoc EMA backbone updates, and final full fine-tuning), accompanied by numerous hyperparameters ($\lambda, \gamma, N_L, N_U, N_a, \alpha, N_c, \lambda_{damp}$). The resulting accuracy improvements (typically +0.1% to +1.5%, with a few reaching ~+2.5%) are relatively modest given the algorithmic complexity.

strengths: The paper introduces an interesting conceptual framework (BiSSL) formulating the transition between self-supervised pretext pre-training and downstream supervised fine-tuning as a bilevel optimization (BLO) problem using implicit gradients.
The mathematical derivation of the upper-level gradient using the implicit function theorem and conjugate gradient (CG) approximation is clear and well-documented.

The method is evaluated across 14 diverse image classification benchmarks, reporting mean and standard deviation over 10 random seeds per benchmark, demonstrating consistent (if modest) gains over standard fine-tuning.
The paper is clearly written, thoughtfully organized, and includes detailed appendices covering hyperparameter selections, algorithm design, and implementation choices.
weaknesses: Lack of essential baselines: The paper only compares BiSSL against standard fine-tuning ('Only FT'). Crucially, it omits comparison against simple joint multi-task learning (co-training the pretext loss and downstream supervised cross-entropy jointly: $\min L^P + \beta L^D$), which is computationally much cheaper than bilevel optimization. It also fails to compare empirically against prior priming techniques mentioned in the related work (e.g., COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE).

High computational cost and lack of efficiency profiling: Approximating the inverse Hessian-vector product via conjugate gradients (Algorithm 2) over multiple iterations introduces substantial memory and runtime overhead. The manuscript provides no wall-clock training times, FLOP comparisons, or memory footprint analyses to demonstrate whether the marginal performance gains justify this computational expense.

Violation of standard SSL transfer practicality: A primary utility of self-supervised learning is that expensive pre-training on large unlabeled corpora is done once, and subsequent adaptation to downstream tasks is fast and lightweight. BiSSL requires retaining and processing the entire pretext pre-training dataset every time a new downstream task is encountered, which significantly limits practical applicability.

Unfair comparison in feature visualization (Section 4.4): The t-SNE analysis compares backbone representations of BiSSL against standard pretext pre-training *prior* to fine-tuning. Because the BiSSL backbone has already been optimized using downstream supervised labels during the bilevel phase, it is expected to exhibit better downstream class separation than an entirely unsupervised pretext backbone.

Limited experimental scale: The empirical validation is restricted to a small ResNet-18 architecture pre-trained on STL-10 (96x96 resolution). Without validation on standard modern SSL benchmarks (e.g., ResNet-50 / ViT on ImageNet-1k), it remains unverified whether BiSSL scales effectively to standard vision workflows.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Framing the interplay between self-supervised pretext pre-training and downstream supervised fine-tuning as a bilevel optimization (BLO) problem provides a fresh perspective on transfer learning in SSL.

Clear mathematical derivation: The derivation of the implicit gradient via the implicit function theorem, regularized lower-level objective, and conjugate gradient approximation (following iMAML-style Hessian-vector products) is mathematically sound and clearly articulated.

Broad evaluation suite: The authors test the proposed framework across 14 distinct downstream classification benchmarks, conducting 10 runs per dataset to report rigorous means and standard deviations.

Comprehensive appendix and qualitative analysis: The paper includes thorough implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and extensive t-SNE visualizations illustrating feature clustering prior to fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Violation of the core SSL paradigm and practical utility: The standard SSL paradigm relies on pre-training once on large-scale unlabeled data, after which the model is lightweightly adapted to diverse downstream tasks without revisiting the pre-training dataset. BiSSL requires concurrent access to the entire pre-training dataset and iterative lower-level pretext steps during downstream adaptation, significantly limiting its practical applicability when pre-training data is proprietary, private, or massive.

Lack of essential baselines: The method is only compared against standard fine-tuning ('Only FT'). It lacks comparisons to standard joint multi-task learning (e.g., simultaneously minimizing L_D + beta * L_P), parameter-regularized fine-tuning (e.g., L2-SP, weight decay toward pre-trained weights), and explicit backbone priming methods discussed in the related work (such as COIN, Noisy-Tune, or RIFLE). Without these comparisons, it is impossible to determine whether the gains stem specifically from the bilevel optimization structure or simply from joint regularization / continuing pretext training.

Omission of computational complexity and wall-clock analysis: Approximating the inverse Hessian-vector product via iterative conjugate gradient (CG) steps over multiple stored batches is computationally demanding. The paper does not report training runtime, GPU memory consumption, or FLOP counts comparing BiSSL against standard fine-tuning or joint training.

Limited scale of models and datasets: Experiments are exclusively conducted with a ResNet-18 on STL-10 images downscaled to 96x96. Given that modern SSL workflows rely on Vision Transformers (ViT) and larger-scale datasets (such as ImageNet-1k), it remains unverified whether this Hessian-based bilevel formulation scales computationally and stably to standard deep architectures.

Marginal empirical improvements on several benchmarks: Across multiple datasets in Table 1 (e.g., STL-10L, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Food-101, Cars), the accuracy gains are marginal (<= 0.3%) or slightly negative, which may not justify the added algorithmic complexity and computational cost of bilevel optimization.

strengths: Novel formulation: Formulating the alignment between self-supervised pretext pre-training and downstream fine-tuning as a bilevel optimization (BLO) problem is an interesting and creative perspective on bridging the domain/task gap in SSL.

Extensive benchmark coverage: The framework is evaluated across 12 diverse downstream image classification benchmarks and an object detection task on PASCAL VOC, spanning two different SSL methods (SimCLR and BYOL).

Substantial empirical improvements: The proposed intermediate stage yields marked improvements over standard fine-tuning on several fine-grained classification datasets (e.g., +9.6% on CUB200, +6.4% on Pets for SimCLR).

Qualitative insights: The t-SNE latent space visual comparisons (Section 4.4 and Appendix C.2) provide helpful intuition demonstrating that class separation is already significantly enhanced prior to supervised fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Lack of essential multi-task / joint-training baselines: The paper justifies bilevel optimization for connecting pretext and downstream objectives, but completely omits comparison to standard first-order alternatives, most notably simultaneous multi-task learning (e.g., optimizing $\mathcal{L}^D + \beta \mathcal{L}^P$) or regularized fine-tuning (e.g., feature distillation / $L_2$-SP). Without these, it is impossible to determine whether the gains come from the bilevel optimization hierarchy or simply from multi-task exposure to both datasets/losses during adaptation.

Absence of direct comparisons with cited backbone priming methods: Section 2 cites multiple relevant techniques designed to bridge pre-training and fine-tuning (e.g., Noisy-Tune, COIN, RIFLE), yet none of these methods are evaluated as empirical baselines in Table 1 or Table 2.

Omission of computational cost and runtime analysis: Bilevel optimization using implicit differentiation and Conjugate Gradient (CG) incurs non-trivial computation due to repeated Hessian-vector products. The manuscript does not report wall-clock time, GPU memory consumption, or relative overhead compared to standard fine-tuning.

Non-standard pre-training resolution and dated architectures: Pre-training ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1K at $96 \times 96$ resolution deviates significantly from standard practice ($224 \times 224$), making comparisons with existing SSL literature difficult. Furthermore, testing is restricted to convolutional networks (ResNet-18/50) without validation on modern Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures or masked autoencoding objectives (e.g., MAE).

strengths: Novel Conceptual Formulation: Framing the transition between self-supervised pre-training and downstream adaptation as a bilevel optimization (BLO) problem provides an interesting alternative to standard sequential pre-train/fine-tune pipelines.
Extensive Downstream Evaluation: The authors evaluate across 12 image classification benchmarks as well as object detection on VOC07+12, covering a broad variety of downstream domains.

Comprehensive Mathematical Formulation: The derivation of the implicit gradient via the implicit function theorem and conjugate gradient approximation is clearly presented and documented in the appendix.
Qualitative Analysis: Latent space visualizations (t-SNE) across multiple datasets offer intuitive qualitative support for improved feature clustering prior to fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Missing Crucial Baselines (Multi-Task Learning and Prior Priming Methods): The central premise of using bilevel optimization over standard optimization is not validated against a simple Joint Multi-Task Learning baseline (i.e., optimizing $\mathcal{L}^D + \alpha \mathcal{L}^P$). Furthermore, despite citing prior backbone priming approaches (e.g., COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE), none are compared empirically to demonstrate whether the computational complexity of BLO provides tangible gains over simpler heuristics.

Computational Cost and Wall-Clock Complexity Unreported: Solving the inverse Hessian-vector product via the Conjugate Gradient (CG) method introduces significant computational and memory overhead. The manuscript does not report wall-clock training times, per-iteration runtime, or peak GPU memory consumption compared to standard fine-tuning or joint training.

Non-Standard Experimental Setup: Pre-training and fine-tuning ResNet-50 on ImageNet at a reduced image resolution of $96 \times 96$ pixels (rather than the standard $224 \times 224$) deviates significantly from standard SSL evaluation protocols, raising questions about whether the observed dynamics and distribution gaps generalize to standard high-resolution pipelines and modern Vision Transformer architectures (e.g., MAE, DINOv2).

Theoretical Disconnects and Heuristic Upper-Level Loss: The theoretical derivation of the implicit gradient assumes the pretext head $\phi_P$ is fixed and that the lower-level problem reaches stationarity, neither of which strictly holds during alternating training. In addition, the upper-level loss heuristically adds $\mathcal{L}^D(\theta_D, \phi_D)$ to improve empirical stability, which blurs the clean bilevel interpretation between $\theta_D$ and $\theta_P$.

strengths: The paper is clearly structured and well-written, with intuitive diagrams (Figure 1) and explicit algorithmic descriptions (Algorithm 1 and 2).

The experimental evaluation is extensive in terms of downstream datasets, covering 12 classification benchmarks and VOC object detection across two popular contrastive/self-supervised learning methods (SimCLR and BYOL).
Comprehensive appendix detailing the mathematical derivations, hyperparameter search spaces, and reproducibility details.
weaknesses: Missing crucial baselines: While the related work discusses several methods for priming pre-trained backbones (e.g., COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE) and joint training, the experimental section only compares BiSSL against standard fine-tuning ('Only FT'). A simple multi-task objective (jointly optimizing downstream supervised loss and pretext loss) or weight-regularized fine-tuning (e.g., L2-SP / weight decay toward initial pre-trained parameters) is not evaluated, leaving it unclear whether the complexity of bilevel optimization is strictly necessary.

Circular evaluation in feature visualization: Section 4.4 and Figures 3, 5–10 compare the t-SNE embeddings of the purely self-supervised backbone against the backbone after BiSSL. Because BiSSL explicitly optimizes on labeled downstream data DD via the upper-level loss, it is expected that the features will cluster according to downstream classes. Framing this as evidence that BiSSL inherently aligns representations before fine-tuning is misleading, as the model has already been exposed to the downstream labels.

Computational overhead and scalability concerns: The bilevel optimization formulation requires computing inverse Hessian-vector products via Conjugate Gradient (5 iterations of second-order backpropagation per upper-level step). The paper does not report wall-clock time, GPU memory consumption, or computational complexity comparisons against the baseline. Furthermore, evaluating only ResNet-50 at a downsampled resolution (96x96) leaves open the question of whether this approach scales to modern vision architectures (e.g., Vision Transformers / ViT) and standard pre-training resolutions (224x224).

Heuristic nature of the formulation: In Eq. (2), the upper-level objective contains both $\mathcal{L}^D(\theta_P^*, \phi_D)$ and $\mathcal{L}^D(\theta_D, \phi_D)$, and the algorithm outputs $\theta_P$ which is subsequently fine-tuned yet again on the downstream task. The theoretical justification for this specific nested setup over standard fine-tuning or existing bilevel meta-learning schemes is limited, and the necessity of the auxiliary term in Eq. (2) is only justified heuristically.
